subarea: Models for wildfires and building fires
statement: BASS-II: in space fuels burn as oval balls, a simpler process used to evaluate fuel-burning computer models that can then study wildfires, building fires, waste-to-energy recapture
BASS: models validated in microgravity flow environment build up to more complex normal-gravity models with wide terrestrial applicability
ACME: improve combustion efficiency and cut pollutant emissions; soot control; oxygen-enriched combustion that could enable carbon sequestration; better models cut combustor design time and cost
ACME project scientist: knowledge can help design furnaces, power plants and boilers that are more efficient, less polluting and safer
Microgravity flames contain 5-8 times more soot than equivalent normal-gravity flames, giving model benchmarks
Highly diluted weak flames are more stable in microgravity, extending dilution limits; useful for stabilization mechanism understanding
FLEX: more efficient and less harmful suppression systems with lower risk of toxic byproducts; relevance to confined or reduced-gravity settings such as submarines and high-altitude aircraft
FLEX cool-flame chemistry matters for internal combustion engines with higher efficiency and lower emissions
Premixed flame work led to a burner with ultra-low pollutant emissions, with application in domestic water heaters and furnaces
Microgravity showed fire-generated particle sizes differ, so detectors tuned to terrestrial smoke may look for the wrong signature

SAME-1 tested 30 samples (6 each of Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose, dibutyl phthalate on wick) on ISS Expedition 15; SAME-2 (Expedition 24, 2010) tested five materials incl. cotton and Pyrell with over 100 samples
ISS detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of tests and Teflon smoke in two-thirds
All fuels produced substantial sub-micron particles; sizes 100-600 nm; Teflon and Kapton smallest

ISS forward light scattering detector (near-IR, most sensitive above 1 micron) had diminished response to Kapton and Teflon smoke under 300 nm; ionization detector responded slightly better, especially to Teflon
Low-gravity smoke count mean diameter about 50% larger than similar normal-gravity conditions
Particle size increases at low flow and with aging; smoke in poorly ventilated enclosures is larger
ISS detector alarm point on the order of 0.5 mg/m3
Alarm threshold reached at 981 s, after most hazardous gas release; PMMA tests exceeded 1-hour CO2 and 24-hour CO limits
ECLSS particle filtration can outpace smoke accumulation in an early small fire, so detection may be delayed
O2 mole fraction 0.10-0.50, suppressant (CO2, He) 0-0.70, pressure 0.5-3.0 atm
Heptane and methanol droplets; determines limiting oxygen index (LOI) and how suppressants shift it
LOI = 0.209 x (1 - MEC)
CO2 is radiatively active and not removed by buoyant convection; also not physiologically inert at extinguishing concentrations
Terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards do not give the same safety margin in low gravity
Local suppressant application is not adequate; jet entrains air and can sustain the flame; nitrogen can strengthen a flame

CO2, N2 and He act as passive suppressants via O2 displacement and cooling; required concentration rises with flow velocity up to about 10 cm/s, where effective enthalpy is near the normal-gravity value
Specification based on NFPA 12: 30% by volume for flaming fires, 50% for smoldering fires with a 20 minute hold
FLEX showed cool flames can burn for a prolonged period after visible flame extinction
Isolation: turn off local power and airflow

subarea: Lunar gravity may be the most flammable condition for some fuels
statement: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests lunar gravity is near the most flammable condition; minimum O2 for flammability near lunar g (model); downward spread rate peaks in partial g

Centrifuge facility showed flammability limits depend on gravity level; most flammable upward spread for certain fuels near lunar g; differences in ULOI and MOC largest at lunar g (table not captured)
Limited data suggest upward spread rate for very thin fuels is proportional to gravity; downward spread is non-monotonic
Fire behavior in partial gravity cannot be expected to be interpolated from 0-g and 1-g
Thin solid upward spread tested at 0.10 g, 0.16 g (lunar), 0.38 g (Martian) and 1 g; extinction pressure depends on gravity and sample width

subarea: Material that burns only in lunar g
statement: SIBAL burns downward in air in lunar gravity but extinguishes right after ignition in Earth gravity
NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is run in 1-g; one source says it is not conservative for microgravity, another says 1-g may not be the most flammable condition (lunar g could be worse)
Material flammability in actual partial gravity is poorly understood; partial-gravity data are limited to aircraft, centrifuge drop rig, LUCI
Four solid samples: two SIBAL burned in air (21% O2, 14.7 psia) and two acrylic rods in 34% O2, 8.2 psia, each upward and downward; CLPS lander CP-21; launch listed as planned for late 2026
A 2024 NASA briefing lists FM2 tests at 37% O2; the FM2 abstract lists 21% and 34%. Treat conditions as unconfirmed until FM2 results are published
In FY2025 researchers ran lunar-gravity and lunar-atmosphere simulation tests in NASA's Zero Gravity Facility (President's Aeronautics and Space Report FY2025)

subarea: LUCI: SIBAL flame base spread rate
statement: 0.9 mm/s (lunar g) vs 1.5 mm/s (1-g); ratio 0.6

subarea: LUCI: SIBAL flame tip spread rate
statement: 1.1 mm/s (lunar g) vs 2.8 mm/s (1-g); ratio 0.39

subarea: LUCI: PMMA rod flame tip spread rate
statement: 0.15 cm/s (lunar g) vs 0.40 cm/s (1-g); ratio 0.38

subarea: LUCI: SIBAL semi-steady flame size in lunar g
statement: about 3.2 cm wide, about 1.5 cm long
1-g extinction occurred about 45 s sooner than in lunar g

subarea: LUCI: Chamber O2 during SIBAL lunar-g burn
statement: fell from about 20% to about 18%

subarea: LUCI: Chamber O2 during PMMA lunar-g burn
statement: fell from 20% to 14.3%
11 RPM rotation, 1.22 m effective radius, lunar-g centrifugal acceleration, normal-pressure air, two samples (SIBAL fabric and 4 mm PMMA rod), burn over 2.5 min; Coriolis force is a stated caveat
quantitative_detail: Coriolis force is a stated caveat

statement: Melamine foam insulation: Acceptable at 30% O2, 10.2 psia; Flammable at 34-40% O2, 8.2 psia; Solimide HT-340 suggested as possible replacement
Nomex: Acceptable to 30% O2, 10.2 psia; Unlikely acceptable at 34-40% O2, 8.2 psia; Fire-retardant treatment may make it acceptable
Portable fire extinguisher (PFE): Will not meet flammability requirements at the highest exploration O2
BPA bladder material: Flammable in ISS environments; used up to 30% O2 at 10.2 psia; Needs additional testing at 34-40% O2, 8.2 psia
Ammonia cartridges for emergency mask: Flammable but acceptable; Acceptable status at 34-40% O2 not established in captured text; Reduced cartridge performance possible at 8.2 psia
General statement: At 34% O2 and 8.2 psia materials that are non-flammable on Earth can become flammable and flammable materials need lower ignition energy; From extinguisher research paper
